Flawed and also powerful, Punch tells an astonishing story, and is a chastening corrective in this era of terrible human behavior.

Based on Jacob Dunne’s memoir, Punch transforms one teen’s deadly mistake into a powerful meditation on justice, grief, and forgiveness.
Punch may have no physical organs but—if you’re willing to stretch the metaphor—you can say it thinks, protects, renews, breathes, and, assuredly, has a beating heart.
It is a wake up call that knocks us out of the park with its message: it’s never too late to be better.
James Graham's astonishing, heartbreaking new play arrives at a time when half the world seems consumed with extracting justice.
It’s a play that lingers like guilt itself—uncomfortable, unresolved, and impossible to shake.
Yes, it’s based on what actually happened, but it involves a whole lot of sitting around and talking, falling short of the knockout blow.
Harrison’s volcanic yet vulnerable performance will not be forgotten by viewers – and hopefully remembered when awards season rolls around next spring.
